title: EC2 — Virtual Machines
subtitle: Launch, connect, and manage virtual machines — AMIs, instance types, security groups, and key pairs

content.text: EC2 — rent a computer in the cloud

EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a virtual machine running in AWS's data center. You choose the operating system (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows), the hardware size (CPU, RAM, storage), and the region. Within minutes, you have a full Linux server you can SSH into, install software on, and run anything — exactly like a physical server, but billed by the hour.

content.code:
FORMAT: family.size
Examples: t3.micro, m7g.large, c7i.2xlarge, r6i.4xlarge

FAMILIES:
  t3/t4g  — General purpose, burstable        → dev/test, low-traffic apps
  m7g/m6i — General purpose, balanced          → most production apps
  c7i/c6g — Compute optimized (more CPU/RAM)   → CPU-intensive workloads
  r7i/r6g — Memory optimized (more RAM/CPU)    → databases, caching
  g4dn    — GPU instances                      → ML inference, video
  i3/i4i  — Storage optimized (NVMe SSDs)      → databases, big data

  Suffix 'g' = Graviton (ARM) — 20-40% cheaper, same performance

SIZES (within a family, each size doubles resources):
  nano → micro → small → medium → large → xlarge → 2xlarge → 4xlarge...

PRACTICAL SIZING (2026 pricing, us-east-1, on-demand):
  t4g.micro   → 2 vCPU, 1GB    → $6/month   (free tier: 750h/month)
  t4g.small   → 2 vCPU, 2GB    → $12/month  (small API, hobby project)
  t4g.medium  → 2 vCPU, 4GB    → $24/month  (Node.js app + workers)
  m7g.large   → 2 vCPU, 8GB    → $56/month  (production API)
  m7g.xlarge  → 4 vCPU, 16GB   → $112/month (higher traffic)

  Spot instances: up to 90% off on-demand, can be interrupted
  Reserved instances: commit to 1-3 years, save 30-60%

content.filename: Launch and connect to an EC2 instance
content.code:
# 1. Create a key pair (to SSH into the instance)
aws ec2 create-key-pair \
  --key-name myapp-key \
  --query 'KeyMaterial' \
  --output text > myapp-key.pem
chmod 400 myapp-key.pem   # restrict permissions

# 2. Create a security group (instance-level firewall)
aws ec2 create-security-group \
  --group-name myapp-sg \
  --description 'MyApp security group'
# Allow SSH from your IP only:
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-name myapp-sg \
  --protocol tcp --port 22 \
  --cidr $(curl -s ifconfig.me)/32
# Allow HTTP/HTTPS from anywhere:
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-name myapp-sg --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-name myapp-sg --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

# 3. Launch the instance
# AMI IDs change by region — get latest Ubuntu 24.04 in your region:
aws ssm get-parameters \
  --names /aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/24.04/stable/current/amd64/hvm/ebs-gp2/ami-id \
  --query 'Parameters[0].Value' --output text

aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx \
  --instance-type t4g.small \
  --key-name myapp-key \
  --security-groups myapp-sg \
  --count 1 \
  --user-data file://startup.sh   # optional: runs on first boot

# 4. Get the public IP
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
  --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].[InstanceId,PublicIpAddress]' \
  --output table

# 5. SSH in
ssh -i myapp-key.pem ubuntu@54.x.x.x

content.text: User data — bootstrap on first boot

content.code:
#!/bin/bash
# This script runs as root on the first boot of the instance
# Use it to install software and configure the server

set -e   # exit on error

# Update packages
apt-get update -y
apt-get upgrade -y

# Install Node.js 20
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_20.x | bash -
apt-get install -y nodejs

# Install Nginx
apt-get install -y nginx

# Install Docker
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
usermod -aG docker ubuntu

# Clone and start the app
git clone https://github.com/myorg/myapp.git /app
cd /app
npm ci --production

# Install PM2 to manage the Node.js process
npm install -g pm2
pm2 start server.js --name myapp
pm2 startup ubuntu -u ubuntu --hp /home/ubuntu  # auto-start on reboot
pm2 save

echo 'Server setup complete'

content.filename: Security group rules for a web server
content.code:
INBOUND RULES (what traffic can reach the instance):
  Type    Protocol  Port  Source
  SSH     TCP       22    Your IP only (x.x.x.x/32) — NEVER 0.0.0.0/0
  HTTP    TCP       80    0.0.0.0/0 (anywhere)
  HTTPS   TCP       443   0.0.0.0/0 (anywhere)
  Custom  TCP       3000  sg-xxxxxxxxx (allow traffic from app LB only)

OUTBOUND RULES (what traffic can leave the instance):
  By default: all outbound is allowed
  Restrict: specific IPs/ports for locked-down environments

Security group rules are STATEFUL:
  If you allow inbound on port 80, the response traffic is
  automatically allowed out — you don't need to add an outbound rule

Never:
  - Allow SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0 — bots scan for this constantly
  - Use security groups as your only security layer
  - Forget to revoke rules when they're no longer needed

content.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead of SSH. Session Manager gives you a shell in your EC2 instance from the AWS console or CLI — no key pairs, no open port 22, no SSH firewall rules. Access is controlled by IAM. It logs sessions to CloudWatch. It works even in private subnets with no internet gateway. It's strictly better than SSH for production access.

questions.question: You add an inbound security group rule allowing port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Do you also need to add an outbound rule for port 80?
options: Yes — you must explicitly allow both directions
No — security groups are stateful; response traffic for allowed inbound connections is automatically allowed out
Yes — but only if the instance sends large responses
Outbound rules don't exist in security groups
questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful. When an inbound connection is allowed, the return traffic for that connection is automatically permitted regardless of outbound rules. This is different from Network ACLs (NACLs), which are stateless and require explicit rules in both directions. This means you only need to think about 'what traffic do I want to allow IN' when configuring security groups — responses take care of themselves.

faq.q: EC2 vs Lambda vs ECS — which compute service should I use?
faq.a: EC2: you manage the OS, best for long-running processes, VMs, or when you need full control. Lambda: for short-lived functions triggered by events, pay-per-invocation, zero servers to manage. ECS/Fargate: for containerized applications, managed container scheduling. Start with Lambda for event-driven code, Fargate for containerized apps, EC2 only when you need specific OS-level control.

examples: GitHub's CI runners are EC2 Spot instances — they use Spot (up to 90% cheaper) because CI jobs can tolerate interruption: if a job gets interrupted, it just restarts
Spot instances saved Netflix an estimated $300M/year when they used them for encoding video — if an encoding job gets interrupted, it restarts from a checkpoint
